title: Good Strategy / Bad Strategy
author: Richard Rumelt
thesisParagraph: Good Strategy / Bad Strategy teaches that strategy is not ambition, vision, targets, or a long list of initiatives. A good strategy starts by facing the real obstacle, finding where power or leverage actually sits, choosing a guiding policy, and coordinating actions so they reinforce one another. Bad strategy hides from the hard part: it uses lofty language, consensus, and activity to avoid diagnosis and tradeoffs. The reader learns to ask what problem governs the situation, what source of power can be used, and what coherent action would make the response real.

coreIdeas.name: Diagnosis before ambition
coreIdeas.oneSentence: A strategy earns the name only when it names the real obstacle instead of decorating hope with goals.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: force every plan to state what problem it is built to overcome

coreIdeas.name: Hidden power
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Strategic force often comes from changing the terms of the contest rather than trying harder on inherited terms.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: look for asymmetry, system advantage, or a pivot point before choosing action

coreIdeas.name: The kernel
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Diagnosis, guiding policy, and coherent action work as one structure, not three separate planning slogans.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: connect the obstacle, the chosen response, and the concrete actions into a chain

coreIdeas.name: Coherence beats initiative piles
coreIdeas.oneSentence: A pile of good-sounding actions can still be bad strategy if the actions do not reinforce one another.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: remove actions that do not serve the governing response

coreIdeas.name: Constraints create focus
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Weak links, proximate objectives, and focus turn vague intent into a near target where effort can matter.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: choose the limiting link or near objective that deserves concentrated force now

coreIdeas.name: Strategic judgment stays active
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Dynamics, inertia, entropy, and analogy risk mean strategy must be reasoned through rather than copied.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: test causal stories against movement over time and resist easy comparisons

targetReader: Managers, founders, operators, civic leaders, consultants, and ambitious individual contributors who are tired of plans that sound impressive but do not change outcomes. They care because the book gives them a way to distinguish real strategic work from activity, consensus, and slogans.

signatureMoves: distinguishes diagnosis, guiding policy, and coherent action with dry precision
spots fluff, proximate objectives, and bad strategy hiding in big words
uses business and policy cases as tests of leverage
keeps the prose skeptical of goals that do not force choices
avoidMoves: Avoid "The point is" as a paragraph hinge.
Avoid "the question is" as a setup crutch.
Avoid triadic abstract-noun lists such as clarity, courage, and resilience.
Do not call ambition a strategy.
Do not let a list of initiatives stand in for a kernel.

voiceSpecimens: A strategy starts with the obstacle, not the ambition.
If the actions do not cohere, the slogan is doing theater.
voiceAntiSpecimens: In this chapter, readers will learn the importance of strategic alignment.
Leaders should leverage holistic frameworks to optimize competitive advantage.
The key takeaway is that good strategy is very important in modern organizations.
Try to be more focused and intentional about your goals.
Strategy is a journey of discovering your best self.
teachingArc: The book starts by separating real strategy from ambition and activity. It then teaches the reader to find power, recognize bad strategy, and build the kernel. The middle chapters turn that kernel into operating judgment: leverage, proximate objectives, weak links, design, focus, growth, and dynamics. The final stretch teaches structural resistance and disciplined thinking so strategy becomes a practice of causal judgment under pressure rather than a document.
forbiddenMoves: Do not turn the book into generic leadership advice about vision, alignment, or execution.
Do not treat every chapter as a synonym for focus; leverage, proximate objectives, design, growth, dynamics, and disciplined thinking each need their own move.
Do not invent detailed Rumelt anecdotes for thin-source chapters.
Do not make examples default to boardrooms, whiteboards, coffee cups, classrooms, or spreadsheet scenes.
Do not use strategy theater vocabulary.
Do not praise alignment without a diagnosis of the obstacle.
